text_translated_detailed: Satria. To the Noble, High, Esteemed Gentlemen The Gentlemen Directors At the Assembly of Seventeen. Representing the General Dutch chartered East India Company Amsterdam. Noble, High, Esteemed, Commanding Gentlemen. — It was on the 30th of December of the recently passed year 1693, when we last had the honor of writing to your Noble High Esteemed Excellencies, and to make briefly known the condition of this coast according to the circumstances of the time, addressed to the Noble Gentleman Extraordinary Councillor of India and Governor, Thomas van Rhee, and Council at Ceylon, in order that with the return ships the Voorboog and Faam your Noble High Esteemed Excellencies would be brought to, and since we have no reason to doubt the safe passage of those vessels (which we hope God the Lord will have granted:) we shall request your Noble High Esteemed Excellencies to graciously accept the copy of that letter enclosed herein, pass by, and respectfully say in this: that we according to our made promise, and highest obligation, have not failed to prepare our further reports, and on the 10th of March of this year per the ship Courtgena with such attachments as pertained thereto, and together copied or prepared, in order to be carried over the land route of Persia in the customary manner to your Noble High Esteemed Excellencies, but since we have had the misfortune that that vessel after three and a half months of struggling, on account of many encountered contrary winds and exceptionally strong currents running to the east, and mistaken course in place of the northern Hook Costa dos Picos, 70 miles lower and near the eastern hook Pica dos Hiljos having fallen, was unable to obtain, for the preservation of ship, men, and goods, it could not be recovered, through weakness of crew since by an extraordinary mortality at the inner water

text_translated_detailed: Gentlemen on the 10th of August 1692 in humble submission. In June 1693 there came again a breach on the waterside on the seaward side of more than 30 feet long, and the collapsed section would have been washed away, had one not been there in time to prevent it. However, the necessary repairs were postponed by the chief van der Duijn in hope that the Commander would personally have come after the passage of the rainy monsoon to provide him with the necessary orders regarding one and another matter. Since this did not happen owing to his indisposition and untimely death, we have deemed it necessary to give your Honorable Gentlemen hereupon in introduction humble advice with most respectful request that your Honorable Gentlemen's order be deigned to be given regarding how we shall conduct ourselves therein and judge to proceed. We would be grateful if you would hold them in favorable regard and honor them with such remaining according to the open deed of your Honorable Gentlemen as is proper. To the clerk of the secretary and secretary of the Council of Justice of this city, under the expectation that he as a person who deserved such would soon be favored with the quality of bookkeeper, but his indisposition and the death that followed having prevented such, we request most humbly that it may please your Honorable Gentlemen to think of him favorably, and with the aforementioned quality together with the ordinary junior merchant's salary. We do not doubt that he will make himself worthy of this kindness. Likewise we request humbly that your Honorable Gentlemen hold in favorable regard the engineer Hans Jungen Tarnant, who was appointed by the Commander as provisional ensign on the 1st of March 1692, and on the 10th of August 1692 requested his position to be confirmed by your Honorable Gentlemen, and since that time has conducted himself well and as a capable officer, thereby meriting your Honorable Gentlemen's favor.

text_translated_detailed: Extracts from the Daily Annotations, Concerning [matters] to be foreseen for the future, and his Excellency to be able to lend the helpful hand in all things. And whereas the Honored Lord Commander was daily growing weaker and was scarcely any longer in a state to sign any ordinances or other documents, the assembly further resolved that the merchant and provisional administrator, with the prior knowledge of the aforementioned Lord Commander, in matters of the general service of the Honored Company which could not at all be delayed, being the same matters of greater decay or neglect, resting in the place of his Excellency's name, would be able to place on passports that were granted to inland vessels, likewise (with prior advice to the council) on documents of sailors and soldiers who, having completed their contracted time, were inclined once more, for the ordinary improvement of two guilders per month, to bind themselves again to the Honored Company. And as the letters for the fatherland with the ration ships were to be sent, his Excellency particularly recommended to ensure that these be dispatched according to their proper course so that they could be disposed of as required, and likewise that the frigate, the wind of which had been mentioned, be completed as quickly as possible. To all of this the council unanimously promised to acquit themselves according to their ability and according to the little experience they had of matters, to do what would seem to be of greatest service to the Honored Company, until such time as his Excellency (as all earnestly wish might happen in a short time) would be restored or at least, by God's grace, brought to a better state, with the request that his Excellency would be pleased to rely upon this. But in order to fulfill his Excellency's desire regarding the dispatch of letters to the fatherland and Batavia according to their best knowledge, they requested that the Lord Commander be pleased to hand over to the secretary

text_translated_detailed: we shall here below only briefly mention what papers and attachments accompany this, namely first a box in which is enclosed an original letter written by the Honourable Commander dated the 22nd of February of this year to your Honour's Excellency, and from Ceylon, since the return ships had already departed, sent back, together with all the documents according to a separate register, belonging thereto. 1. Copy of a missive dated the 27th and April last from Bassaloor, dispatched by yacht Zillida to Persia in order to be forwarded from there by land to your Honour's Excellency, together with the pertaining attachments. 2. The same, draft of a letter written by His Excellency to her Honour's Excellency to Batavia, now being continued by us according to our ability, and to be dispatched as soon as possible by the frigate the Wind, together with various attachments, according to a particular register. 3. The same, meditated resolutions proposed by His Excellency since the 3rd of August to the 17th of September of this year, together with the written advice of the political members and the conclusion following thereon, concerning principally the matters of the merchant Babba Porboe, who until today is staying at Pananij at the court of the Company's Sammorin, meanwhile the trade here by his son Nannoeponboe according to the aforementioned resolutions until further disposition of her Honour's Excellency is continued in his father's place. 4. Exchanged copies of letters between the Honourable Commander and the aforementioned merchant Babba Porboe. 5. Extracts from the political minutes kept in council of Malabar from the 5th to the 24th of September of the aforementioned year, starting, concerning principally the merchant and former administrator Abraham Vink. 6. Two copies of protests by the Honourable Commander aforementioned sent to the Portuguese governor to Goa concerning a certain hostile treatment by one of their Company's ships committed against the yacht

text_translated_detailed: March also employed all practicable means to completely dominate the Cochin kingdom and bring it entirely under tribute, yet nothing could be done in this regard for the time being, but everything had to be awaited, just as happened through his Highness's forbearance, especially since he was shown the power that the Company had possessed in former times, to impose laws upon the Sammorin, and how in such a case, if necessity required it, their Excellencies would likewise not lack the same means. From this perspective, then, neither could nor would his Highness (as acknowledging their Excellencies' benefactions to the kingdom of Cochin, particularly to his person and his subjects, and recognizing their Excellencies' great power) undertake anything outside the pleasure of the Company. But now one could observe a notorious principle of the threatening evil, which one had always feared, whereby it could be clearly measured what reliance could be placed upon the Sammorin and his word, as it was directly opposed to the interest of his kingdom. And since it was no longer time to sit idle, as the northern lords cried out for murder and burning to come to their aid, and the Sammorin was taking away the entire northern part and the principal portion of the Cochin kingdom, his Highness requested that the President and Governor Alexander Wigmans with the friends of the council would be pleased to come to him, so that they might deliberate upon this matter and reach a salutary decision. Meanwhile, we also received a decree from the Sammorin, together with a letter from the merchant Babba Porbol from Pananij [Panani], by which not only was confirmed the acceptance of the Namboeddij by the Sammorin, but also this prince had decided within a few days to come with the necessary force to attack the Cochin northern lord Moerianattoe Nambiaar, which is the other pillar of the Cochin kingdom, in his own land and bring it under obedience, and likewise to take Combottoe

text_translated_detailed: High and Esteemed [Gentlemen], the election has been made of the persons of the Esteemed Commandeur of Jaffanapatnam [Jaffna], Floris Blom, as Commissioner; the Esteemed Chief Merchant, formerly pro-administrator in Surat, Adriaan van Ommen, as Commandeur; and the Chief Merchant and warehouse master at Colombo, Pieter Coesaart, as second [in command] and administrator of this Malabar Commandery. Furthermore, all orders from Your High and Esteemed [Gentlemen] shall come to us through their gracious Excellencies with all promptitude. The reason why this could not have been dispatched earlier is the receipt of a letter from the Calicoilander [ruler of Calicut], in which he relates his difficulties, which must be followed and obeyed, as well as those which Your High and Esteemed [Gentlemen] may later see fit to dispatch to us according to our regulations. And to inform Your High and Esteemed Gentlemen: since this [letter], as was mentioned here before, was prepared some days ago but could not be sent because in the meantime important matters had come to us beforehand, which required Your High and Esteemed [Gentlemen's] knowledge, as the thorough investigation of matters and the drafting thereof consumed some days, while also some further matters concerning the land affairs have come to us, from which we shall give Your High [Excellency] the due knowledge. text_translated_detailed: Lieutenant Governor of the Coast of Malabar, Canara, and Wingurla, together with the Council. — Most earnest, valiant, very wise, aforementioned, and very esteemed Lord. — In all my letters I have poured out my complaints before your Excellency regarding the detention of two of my vessels and goods at Jaffanapatnam; but since I have received an answer from your Excellency with great comfort and promised instructions, which I have no doubt whatsoever were given, I hoped that these matters would be arranged in time according to right and offered satisfaction, so that the damage, shame, and dishonor might be avoided. This being so, I received after some days a letter to me from my authorized agent at Jaffanapatnam, from which to my particular astonishment it appeared that after all those same goods had been sold at auction, and payment had been given to the Prossidido with the Brahmin carpenter, from his share which I, according to his statement, have under my control, just as the same letter here passes on to my son Nannoe to be read and shown before your Excellency, and recently a vessel of mine with salt and sandalwood, under proper written permission granted by your Excellency, having been sent toward Manapaar, all the sandalwood has been seized and carried away by the Company's servants as soon as it was unloaded, so that I do not know or can think how I have it, on the one hand I am encouraged by your Excellency and the gentlemen of Batavia, under promises that in time they will remember to keep me in my former zeal and to regard the greatest benefit and well-being of the Company's trade, on the other hand all the damage and shame that can be imagined is inflicted upon me by the Company's own ministers, and wherever I lodge a complaint there I receive equal justice, and although such a thing makes a man despair, nevertheless I find it good to write about this to your Excellency and therefore seek your good advice, how I should conduct myself herein for the recovery of the damage and affronts that have been brought upon me, so that I may then be able to direct myself toward the prevention of the ruin that is promised me hereby; Meanwhile, your Excellency is made known that the day before yesterday the second English resident, Mister Thomas Patthe, has arrived here from Calicut, in order to enter into a proper contract with the native merchants at 18 Dutch ducats per candy, which is being pursued by him with all haste to send a ship of theirs that lies at Talichery with that Corevol [uncertain: possibly a type of vessel or cargo] toward Persia, which in my opinion is damage to the Company, since they go with the first market wind, now that the Corevol is very much drawn and required there, which your Excellency is very well aware of. and it is equally known to everyone what damage at Jaffanapatnam [Jaffna] and Nagapatnam [Nagapattinam] has been brought upon me and inflicted by the Company's servants, so that if those gentlemen of conscience could come to see these things, they would confess alongside the infallible truth that they have dealt with me most unjustly, which Your Esteemed Excellency himself shall have to testify, if Your Esteemed Excellency investigates and considers the reasons that were found to hold a sale of my vessel and goods at Jaffanapatnam [Jaffna], although such an occurrence makes a person despondent, nevertheless the damage grieves me not so much as the reproach that I must endure from everyone, for beyond the manifold shames brought upon me by the Company's ministers, I have had to tolerate much more for their Excellency's sake from other nations, as Your Esteemed Excellency, if I trust, shall already be informed, which has befallen me through the Portuguese and their wickedness; yet although such a reward for my good service has been applied to me both by the Company's servants and by others, nevertheless I shall not cease to expend my customary zeal in their Excellency's service, as a demonstration of my steadfast love, concerning their Excellency's trade and further interests, to help advance them as much as it lies in my power, hoping that the High Esteemed Excellency gentlemen of the Indian government will not fail to hold me in favorable thoughts for this, as their Esteemed Excellency's valued missive has given me sufficient assurance thereof; text_translated_detailed: ...and a portion of pepper, without specifying the quantity, to which I added separately something that I had discussed verbally with him, to which I gave him the answer that the aforementioned merchant was not able to deliver it, nor did he know how to provide him with it soon, noting that the Company's business at Surat could be greatly hindered thereby, just as happened when their spices at Cochin were [affected] during the time of the Honorable Lord Lobs. The Honorable Lords of the Indian Government [in Batavia] were very displeased over the complaints made by the Honorable Lord Director and Council at Surat, but since they intend, as I have been directed through the mediation of others, to obtain the same from Cochin or Cannanore, I deem it necessary to advise Your Honorable Excellencies of this. In the meantime, my request is that Your Honorable Excellencies show assistance to my son, Nannoeporboe, who will occupy my position until my arrival there, in all things, and also to be favorable and tolerant in whatever may be lacking to him. With this I conclude, Your Honorable Excellencies' esteemed person commended to God's safe keeping, I remain—(signed) Your Honorable Excellencies' humble and obligated servant, was signed in Canarese characters, Babba Porboe—At the side, Panani, 25th September, year 1694. P.S.: The Company's particularly mighty friend, the Sammorin, I have on your Honorable Excellencies' behalf greeted in a friendly manner by means of this same [letter], and by this same [letter] your Honorable Excellencies' very esteemed messenger has been notified. After the certainty, he asked me whom your Honorable Excellencies, in my opinion, should write to. To the Company's foremost merchant Babba Porboe.—Good friend.—Your two pleasant letters dated the 22nd and 25th with an appendix of the 27th current I have indeed received and gladly understood from it the delivery of my writings 16 and previously dated, thanking you hereby in a friendly manner for your kind wishes of good fortune in my newly undertaken command. Regarding the repetition of your complaints concerning the injustice done at Naga and Jaffanapatnam and the seizure of your vessels and goods, please be assured that I shall not fail to see to it that you receive full satisfaction, just as there is no doubt that the Honorable Excellencies at Batavia will also order the same in such a manner. Therefore I request that you be pleased to remain calm in this regard, and in any case not allow yourself to be stopped by the difficulty that has arisen from such a small principal matter, and to delay longer in coming here, in order that, having held private consultation with the other [officials] concerning many more important matters, both concerning trade as well as the differences between the Honorable Company, the Queen of Attinga, and some other southern princes, we may come to a salutary conclusion. Therefore you will undoubtedly see this as soon as possible, since the matters can no longer bear delay, and therefore I would indeed wish that you would be pleased to declare yourself positively whether you are inclined to come or not able to come, in order that according to the orders and intent of the Honorable Excellencies at Batavia, who expressly desire the matters to be directed with your further assistance, they may be grasped and executed at hand first, and if your arrival should come to be delayed longer, we as the Company shall proceed with it so that the Honorable Company should not suffer any arrears, without it being necessary that you bring any troops or soldiers of the Sammorin with you, such as you have previously proposed to the council, and now in his letter further urged to do, but if there were any reasons, unknown to me, by which you were diverted or held back from coming here, I assure you by this in my capacity as Commander representing the supreme authority on this coast of Malabar, and on the trust of my word, that you, being here, shall not encounter or experience the least adversities or affronts, but on the contrary all honor, respect, and regard shall be shown and given to you, without any diminishment in the same manner, and just as it was at the time and upon the presence here of the Honorable Esteemed Lord Commissioner Hendrik Adriaan van Reede tot Drakenstein, Lord of Mydrecht, etc. (L.M.), and thereafter by the late Honorable Lord Commander J.S. van Dielen, shall be continued, upon which you may freely rely, and as a sign and proof of my goodwill I am sending you hereby a bottle of good tea, which

text_translated_detailed: Translation of a letter, by the Esteemed Mister Commandeur Adriaan van Ommen, to the King Sammorijn, sent on the 24th of September, year 1694. It shall have become known to your Highness how I have arrived here in the city of Cochim from Batavia [Jakarta:], according to my previous written notification. I am fully prepared to maintain good correspondence with your Highness regarding the friendship that exists between your Highness's realm and the Esteemed Company. With my arrival here I have also brought a letter from their High Excellencies in Batavia, to hand over to your Highness as proof of their Excellency's goodwill. Now I wish that your Highness would be pleased to choose a good opportunity to come to Cranganoor [Kodungallur:] as soon as possible, so that I may meet with your Highness and hand over the aforementioned gift together with the letter, and further speak of necessary matters. And since I assure myself that your Highness will not be negligent in this, I remain awaiting your answer to this with longing, may God preserve your Highness, etc. Translation of a letter by the King Sammorijn to the Esteemed Mister Commandeur, written and received on the 4th of December, year 1694. text_translated_detailed: I have received, and read the same with great pleasure, containing such assurances regarding the preservation of our mutual friendship as one could desire. Having also never had any other expectation, and in order through outward duty performance to confirm this reciprocally further and to cause the friendship to grow more and more, my endeavor has been to meet your Highness at Cranganoor. But I have understood to my great sorrow that your Highness could not yet come to Cranganoor for the first time, and therefore I was glad that you came to Pananij, to which I am entirely inclined. But the service of the Esteemed Company cannot permit this, given the great occupations concerning the provision and arrangement of so many important matters which in no way can be postponed without great delay. Therefore the meeting must remain postponed until your Highness shall have completed the ceremonies being undertaken and the feast of Mamangam. In the meantime, we hereby add our thanks for the goodwill shown. So further, this serves to make known to your Highness that upon our arrival here we have caused the Princess of Aringen [uncertain: location/title] to understand the many unreasonable procedures committed successively against the Esteemed Company and demanded satisfaction (among which is also included the elephant brought forward for your Highness), and her Highness having made an offer to give full satisfaction, we have resolved to go in person to the South to accommodate everything amicably with that Princess. Since your Highness is in a very close connection with the Esteemed Company and is particularly interested in this matter, with the request that your Highness believe to send two prominent trusted men of required capacity hither to attend to the matters and help advance them. When we do not doubt a good success to the general satisfaction, to that same end we remain the Company's foremost merchant Babbapor

As they had done in the lodge, they broke open the warehouse and robbed that as well. They have not left me a single copper basin, no hat nor bedding, nor anything of household goods. Whatever did not suit them they broke to pieces. The heaviest goods still lie in the warehouse where they keep watch, and also guard us. They have not even left us food provisions, for which reason from this evening with our entire family we have had to fast. Tomorrow I shall have to speak to good people, if they can be found. Please let us know what is best for us to do, for there is nothing for us to do here at present. I have been unable to obtain any reasons from them other than that the interpreter Joan Fernando shot at them, and that I was of his people. text_translated_detailed: The King Kelorma sent an ola [a letter or proclamation], and thereby complained solely about how the Company's lodge had been so shamefully robbed at Tenkapatnam. What we receive in answer to this, we shall be able to inform Your Excellency about shortly. Through the interpreter Ingenatio de Costa to Coijlan de Sima, we had the robbery acknowledged by the pooles [local chiefs/rulers] who were there. He was present with the poole Debariatte and the poole of Wanjemonton, being the second great poole of Atinge, both of whom showed themselves extremely upset. And when the name of one was called Ragiadoor, they said immediately that this was arranged by Kelormo and no one else, who seeks to make the Company our enemy so that we fall upon them. We shall not rest until they completely restore the Company's residence as it was, or we shall rather abandon our place here entirely. And the aforementioned interpreter said again that they would acknowledge that they would not fail in this, so that we could be at ease. He said again that he had come only to complain about the injustice that had occurred and to advise. Item, from and as before, under date 4th of September, year 1694, signed. To the Honored Hendrik Vockestaart, Under-merchant and President's Commander of the Southern Malabar. — Your Esteemed pleasant letters from the last [dispatch] have come to me well through the dispatched Noelias and Lascorin, and besides that I also received a package of cloth, a hat, shirts, &c., for which I thank your Excellency most heartily. However, I cannot use the same, since I am not yet free of those scabies. Therefore, outside the house, along with other old rags that were given back to me on the first day, [I have] stored [them], for daily they come to sniff around and what pleases them, they take as their own. At Cocatte they have not found much. Twelve loads of coolies they caught on the road from Coijlan. The rest have scattered. This morning they came to take a party of gunny sacks from the warehouse to pack the robbed linens to bring to the Queen, who was disturbed by the delay, and as it is said, she had a package intercepted that the Poele would have sent ahead to his house. Whereupon here 300 Nairs were sent along with some rajahdoors to intercept everything they have robbed. Nelaschar they have put in chains, for he also brought his share to a corner. Now we may hope that within 2 to 3 days that rabble shall depart from here, so that we shall get a little rest. It seems that they now want to make themselves weary here in order to give themselves up, but without order such a thing shall not happen, or they must force us to depart by violence. For if the English were to stick their nose in here, the Company's linen trade would be finished both here and at Cocatte. Therefore I do not doubt that the Company shall be beforehand. The arduin stones fail us; 10 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] for one fan [uncertain: unit of measurement], but we cannot sell any.

text_translated_detailed: It appears that they now wish to make trouble here, in order to get their own way, but without orders such a thing will not happen, or they will have to force us to depart, for if the English were to stick their nose in here, then the Company's linen trade would be finished both here and at Cottatte [Kottayam]. Therefore I do not doubt that the Company will be compensated beforehand. The brick stones are selling at 10 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] per fan [modern equivalent: unit of weight/measure], but we cannot get any buyers for them, as has been mentioned thus far in your esteemed further writings of the third of this month. I have no doubt that your esteemed letter of the 2nd of this month will also have reached me. I have also received a letter for our interpreter, but I cannot yet learn where he is. Nevertheless, I believe it cannot be far away. Our Thomas Aratje arrived here on the evening of the 3rd, and according to what he said, he endured great trouble and hardship, for he had sat in the countryside for three days and eaten rice at night in Schanas' houses. But I asked him whether the esteemed Company had given him provisions for so long, so that in time of need he could hide in the countryside. So he has gone off again with his fat, corpulent brother-in-law. As I understand it, they have gone to Travancore [Thiruvananthapuram]. The letter for Monommeda will be arranged. Therefore I do not doubt that the Company will be compensated beforehand. The brick stones are selling at 10 stuivers small Dutch coins per fan unit of weight/measure, but we cannot get any buyers for them, as has been mentioned thus far in your esteemed further writings of the third of this month. I have no doubt that your esteemed letter of the 2nd of this month will also have reached me. I have also received a letter for our interpreter, but I cannot yet learn where he is. Nevertheless, I believe it cannot be far away. Our Thomas Aratje arrived here on the evening of the 3rd, and according to what he said, he endured great trouble and hardship, for he had sat in the countryside for three days and eaten rice at night in Schanas' houses. In the meantime, there now passes over to your esteemed honors a copy of a further brief letter dated the 7th of this month from the resident Jan Bartelsz., by which your esteemed honors will see how he is still plagued more and more, and it appears from that as if it is beginning to lean toward one side. (in margin:) Tengapatnam the 7th December, Year 1694 — Extract from the letter In answer From here dated the 14th December 1694: to Coijlan Gentlemen signed Your Excellency's letter dated the 9th of this month we have here received at the proper time, and from it we learned how the crossing vessels had been made ready to set out to sea our much-needed advice to their High Lordship, Esteemed and Honored, at Batavia, with the unreliable land route, to be carried over sea to Mannapar; which we hope will already have taken effect before the receipt of this. And further finding nothing particular therein, except the further doings of the audacious robbers of the Company's Lodge at Tengapatnam, regarding which Your Excellency has already been given the necessary orders in our previous writings, so this now serves only as an accompaniment to the packet going herewith, deduced to the Noble Lord, Ceylon's Governor and Council, to the end that by Your Excellency over the land route to Madure as speedily as possible be allowed to proceed. We doubt not in the least that the same, being of small bulk, shall obtain unhindered passage. — Remaining Your Excellency's proposal to hold in abeyance the vessels which in the past good season to the Coast of Coromandel and Jaffanapatnam, by the Company, standing under the rule of Coilang de Sima, have been dispatched, upon their return to be seized, until we shall have received the required advice from the Noble Lord Governor and Council at Ceylon, on the accompanying letter, which for that purpose is being dispatched. — And so forth. text_translated_detailed: dated the 1st of September, in the year 1694, to Cochim. The day before yesterday we received writings from the resident J. Bartelsz. from Tenkapatnam dated the 27th of this month, of which the copy is hereby passed on to Your Excellencies, from which Your Excellencies will come to understand. Since the aforementioned resident's latest writings, he has not been troubled by the Atingse people anymore; undoubtedly because nothing remained, yet it seems the aforementioned resident has received no assurance from anyone that he will remain unmolested. This comes down to the fact that the Atingse Queen has sold our goods to the English friends. We have also heard from Ansjenga that the residence was carried away from there in part to Bettoe. How the merchants near Tenkapatnam are trying to make themselves practically useful with passports from Tutucorijn [Tutucorijn], Your Excellency will also see from the aforementioned copy of writings, which gives reason to fear that those of Alinghe will also seek to do the same as principal. The Moor Ottoman, through the actions of the Madura Moor Peritambij, which, as it is rumored, he would have done before. The Atingse Queen is expected to return to Coijlan Sima in a few days, and will also bring a good number of people with her for the continuation of the war against those of Signatij [uncertain: possibly a place name], great efforts being made to oppose us. With this in mind, the young King of this realm is busy daily making a new fortification, with which on the river side, a piece some distance outside his old work has sprung out, so that the aforementioned Coijlan Sima can now fire upon it from there with the cannon strongly and force it, and it is also rumored that an invasion from there is to be made, so that they are so pressed, that if those of Atingse do not come to their aid with good force, they are to be feared. Poele de Bariatte, with all his subordinates, is seen as subjected and made obedient to this King. Coijlan. To the Honorable Hendrik Vockestaart, etc.

Coijlan To His Excellency Hendrik Vockestaart, under-merchant and provisional governor of the Lower Malabar. Both of Your Excellency's agreeable letters of the 17th and 20th of this month have reached me at their proper time, in which latter it has become clear to me the correct sum of our remaining balance from the end of July, to which the small amount of sold spialter and fabrics is still to be added; I will not doubt that satisfaction will eventually be obtained for all the robberies that have been committed in such a shameful manner by the high-handed King for some time now. text_translated_detailed: Translation of letter by His Excellency the Commander Adriaan van Ommen, etc., to the King of Attingen, the 18th of November 1694. With my arrival here from Batavia in place of the deceased Honored Commander Isaac van Dielen—to hold the supreme authority over the coasts of Malabar, Canara, and Wingurla as absolute Commander—which was on the 11th of this current month, it seemed very strange to me to hear and understand from the Company's servants here how Your Highness had not denied the Honored Company various affronts and insults, namely open violence and hostile acts, such as the striking and arresting of various packages of the Company's linen, areek [betel nut], and tobacco, as well as an elephant which was sent for the King Sammorin of Jaffanapatnam, and most recently the plundering and robbing of the Company's means and effects in the lodge at Tengapatnam. And moreover, that Your Highness would have granted strange nations in your kingdom free passage and free possession to conduct their trade there and to transport pepper. And since such doings and dealings come directly into conflict with all the bonds and Contracts between Your Highness and the illustrious Company, established from of old and recently renewed when Your Highness came to Cochin, I have therefore wished to admonish Your Highness herewith in a friendly manner and to request that Your Highness would please consider and take care that the Honored Company be given proper satisfaction and compensation for all the aforementioned offenses, so that all the unrest, discord, and other misfortunes which might otherwise spring forth from this could be removed and prevented in time. Moreover, henceforth between Your Highness and the Honored Company, according to the content of the aforementioned Contracts, a good harmony and friendship should be maintained and continued.

Herewith having declared our intention in the service of the Company to your Excellency's regulation, we leave the execution of the same to the greatest benefit of their Excellencies under the oath by which we and you are bound, commended, and we wish you, under God's guidance, a speedy journey and completion of affairs, remaining (understood) your well-wishing friends. This serves to inform you that we concluded a small contract here yesterday, amounting to eight thousand pagodas, by which all our Japanese copper and tin have been disposed of, and we would have wished for more of it, as there were still some 500 chests of copper that could have been requested by the merchant, but since we feared that more trade would be lost thereby, we shall nevertheless make it our duty, as time and circumstances permit, to look into this matter so that we can serve the future therein. The necessary oil up to 150 loads we have had you procure (at the best price) by our presence. The commander, as the orders in that regard given in Cochin, shall hand over to you. Our wish shall be that the trade goods there in being may be drawn out and sold, especially those merchant goods which have now lain for a full year (and have been subjected to the weather) so that they come out of hand, in order that His Excellency's Company be freed from damage with the utmost effort, as we shall not doubt in that regard from you. We expect to see you by mid-April as well as after Coudewast [uncertain: possibly a place or time reference], assuring you that we shall be able to bring off the goods before then, for which reason the provision of the much-needed provisions there shall be prepared on our part so that upon our arrival no delay or hindrance shall be caused in that regard, and through the late season the Company suffer no damage (which God forbid). Furthermore, remain commended to God, and with cordial greetings I remain, Your good friend (was signed) M. D. Lonsbeek, at the time at Ancola, 6th of March in the year 1694. From which it appears that we did not authorize the Resident Wijnhout to enter into a contract with the government, but rather that we recommended to him the procurement of the 150 loads of rice against our arrival, since the Company, if one had to wait there on account of the late season, could suffer damage; and it was to be feared that the trade goods there in being, the sale of them, could be consumed, especially those which have now lain for a full year out of the warehouse and have been mostly subjected to the weather; but to our great surprise we learned from the letter from the aforementioned Resident in reply sent to us that he had become a new contract of merchant goods to the amount of 12,320 pagodas with the merchant Cusnapaija [Cusnapaija],

However, we were unable to determine the exact quantity of what had been contracted, and we dared not give the merchant more since he had no more ready cash than the amount of that which was at hand, notwithstanding that he requested this urgently with the assurance that it would not fail, if we would only seek to request a few more days to fully satisfy the contract. But the lateness of the season, as it was then ready until the 12th of April for our maritime affairs to depart, without however being able to do anything against it except to exert all our strength to settle accounts with the merchant as soon as possible, caused us to resolve to settle everything and depart from there. But on the day of our departure, there came to us the captain general and admiral of the Sunda Strait, a Mr. Bullerghan, who had been sent out with a fleet of armed vessels against those of Sambagel Rogia, requesting in the name of the Governor of Coudewaen (called the aforementioned Governor, who had previously been made known to us through various distinguished persons) that we might be able to meet his Excellency there under the presentation of our ships with his armed vessels that he had with him to escort us, and that we would not be detained there, but would obtain speedy progress in trade. Indeed, he assured us that over 5,000 pagodas [modern equivalent: a former monetary unit] had been reckoned for merchants or trading, and in short, unfailingly merchants from the Upper Lands would come down. To this we answered that gentleman in a learned manner, that we thanked the Governor for the favorable proposal this time in a friendly manner, since good sailing weather had already been promised, and stormy weather was at hand at all hours, and therefore we were unable to proceed further northward, with the promise that we would according to our respective duties inform him of this, not doubting that when we might be sent back in good sailing weather, that would be more convenient, and then we would wait with confidence to see whether trade in the Banda lands through the Company's servants could be conducted peacefully; to which end it would not have been bad for the service of the general Company if we had departed from here two or three months earlier, for it is well known to your Excellency how these inland merchants conduct their trade from day to day, dragging it out. Furthermore, here with the aforementioned Mr. Admiral Bullenghan

text_translated_detailed: Oral Report given by the esteemed Captain Lieutenant Cornelis Blik, [uncertain: 1 9n ns Lant], and the messrs. Zeendk Blanckert and Louis [uncertain: ge Taijspel], Purser [expanded: Purveyor] and undercook, all members of the political Council, regarding their negotiation with the Raja of Calicut and Ponca. The aforementioned commissioners, on the 17th of October according to the resolution taken in the Council of the day before, having set out on their journey, arrived on the 19th at Calicut, of which the Raja was immediately informed, with the request that they might obtain an audience at the earliest. His Highness found himself sufficiently inclined, setting the day for the following day, when the envoys went to His Highness's ordinary court in the morning, and there meeting His Highness, they were received very kindly by His Highness and brought to the usual place of audience. After the customary compliments had been made and the gifts that had been brought were offered, which were gratefully accepted by His Highness, His Highness himself began to relate the reasons and motives that had resulted from the disputes between the Princess of Alingen and that of Signasij, namely that the lands of Perisolij had of old been divided into two lordships, under the designation of Perischen Vledettasoru Wan. The first belonged to the Raja of Perisolij, the other had a special administrator, who, having died without legitimate heirs, caused the King of Levancoor as well as the Raja of Perisolij to make claims to it. These two competitors having come into dispute over it, a war broke out between them, which lasted for several years. They were finally brought to an accommodation through the mediation of the Rajas of Calicut and Signasij, with the condition and agreement that the King of Levancoor would always be the first person in

text_translated_detailed: Let it be known that all negotiations with His Highness declined at that time, until His Highness came to provide complete satisfaction to the Company. In such a way that in the absence thereof, His Highness might be obliged to join with those of the Company in order to seek rightful revenge thereupon, being thus bound to His Excellency. And if His Highness were so inclined, the presentation of His Highness's apology and assurance in that matter would have to be made, when His Highness would take the trouble upon himself to persuade the Company to come to an accommodation, by which His Highness meant to have acted prudently for two reasons. First: on account of the costs of stubbornness and orders from the High Indian Government arriving at Batavia to maintain the contracts regarding the trade in weapons with great justice, which could make such matters work, and if not, and His Highness making some good offer in the meantime, we could make use of that, with the declaration that His Excellency would not abandon any reasons in the world to neglect the interest of the Company, to which the welfare of His Highness was committed to help secure to the utmost of his ability, and also not so heavily would it be to neglect his own concerns according to the feeling of another, denoting also the neighboring Rajas, which on the other side the Portuguese, whom he well knew would not gladly see, the Lords of the Coromandel Coast came out too high, yet fell too low, in order to come better under their interest to pursue the goods of India. His Highness is endowed with sufficient knowledge to use this consideration and to be able to prefer the heaviest to the light. Yet His Highness would hold himself as much as possible in appearance reluctant to keep us in friendship with the Raja.

text_translated_detailed: Whom he well knew would not gladly see, the Lords of the Coromandel Coast came out too high, yet fell too low, in order to come better under their interest to pursue the goods of India. His Highness is endowed with sufficient knowledge to use this consideration and to be able to prefer the heaviest to the light. Yet His Highness would hold himself as much as possible in appearance reluctant to keep us in friendship with the Raja of Cochin [Kochi], so that then through that prince, who is now in great difficulty, he might be brought the sooner to a reasonable satisfaction regarding the present actions. Yet the principal game in this matter that the Raja's ambassador had discovered from His Excellency was this: that His Highness could not see with great certainty that the King Sammorin [Zamorin] would be willing or able to help the Company here, for His Highness had made it sufficiently known that such a part ought to happen since the Sammorin broke the contract with the Company's Commissioner (His Majesty) with the honorable Excellency, the aforementioned French lord as an untrustworthy Nambeddy [a title of nobility], His Highness had sought out, and following that the Sammorin also was not to be trusted. text_translated_detailed: Proposal and approval by the Commander and Council, by means of a verbal report and disclosure here, regarding the present condition of the fortification works, as well as dwellings and warehouses there, in order to proceed with the necessary repairs, according to the authority of His Excellency the Governor-General in Batavia, so that they could make decisions and issue orders thereto, as would be found to be appropriate. Also, there was read in the meeting the letter from the merchant Babba Porboe in response to the writing of the Esteemed Commander from Panani, dated the 22nd of this month, sent here; and since it appeared from this that the same person did not seem inclined to come here yet, unless one would consent to his previous proposal, that he would come with some troops of the King Sammorin to continue the war against [uncertain: original text], but since this could in no way be reconciled with the interests of the Esteemed Company, it was therefore unanimously decided to serve him with such a response by letter as soon as possible, and to give him clear signs, so that he might be drawn away from that intention, and through a second invitation in polite and friendly terms be persuaded to present himself here in person alone, so that, with the passage of time, without long delay, as much for the benefit of the trade as for other matters of state, one could confer with him orally, and thus be able to draw a salutary resolution regarding one matter and another, in consideration of the greatest service of the Esteemed Company. Furthermore, by petition presented in Council by the provisional Lieutenant Johannes Sevo, requesting that from the time that his salary was stopped by His Excellency the Governor-General, his allowance for cost money and wine ration might also be validated, this was granted to him as a fair matter, except that in place of heavy money, as requested, he shall have to content himself with light money, and furthermore it was understood that the assistant Hendrik Dirksz. Nooteman, upon his petition presented with the good testimony of his superiors, should be appointed as absolute assistant at 24 [uncertain: currency/measurement] per month under a five-year contract, to perform his service as garrison bookkeeper at the fortress Cannanore. Item: to the widow Joanna d'Aroeje, according to the act of survivance granted to her by the late Esteemed Commissioner Hendrik Adriaan van Reede tot Drakenstein, Lord of Meidrecht, etc., as a widow in place of the deceased Pauladias, monthly from the Company's treasury for her maintenance to be provided, four rixdollars [modern equivalent: a currency unit], for which she shall also remain obliged to present herself always, at the service of any of the inhabitants of this state, whenever they should have need of her assistance. Thus done, decided, and resolved within the city of Cochin on the day, month, and year aforementioned, was signed: Adriaan van Ommen, President; Coesaart; D. de Chavonnes; A. Wighm; J. Also, there was read in the meeting the letter from the merchant Babba Porboe in response to the writing of the Esteemed Commander from Panani, dated the 22nd of this month, sent here; and since it appeared from this that the same person did not seem inclined to come here yet, unless one would consent to his previous proposal, that he would come with some troops of the King Sammorin to continue the war against original text, but since this could in no way be reconciled with the interests of the Esteemed Company, it was therefore unanimously decided to serve him with such a response by letter as soon as possible, and to give him clear signs, so that he might be drawn away from that intention, and through a second invitation in polite and friendly terms be persuaded to present himself here in person alone, so that, with the passage of time, without long delay, as much for the benefit of the trade as for other matters of state, one could confer with him orally, and thus be able to draw a salutary resolution regarding one matter and another, in consideration of the greatest service of the Esteemed Company. Nooteman, upon his petition presented with the good testimony of his superiors, should be appointed as absolute assistant at 24 currency/measurement per month under a five-year contract, to perform his service as garrison bookkeeper at the fortress Cannanore. Thus done, decided, and resolved within the city of Cochin on the day, month, and year aforementioned, was signed: Adriaan van Ommen, President; Coesaart; D. de Chavonnes; A. Wighm; J.
